prompt:
You are evaluating a source-code privacy technique. Your job is to defeat it. A tool called `effigy` takes a source file from some **original problem domain** and rewrites or obscures it so the file can be sent to a third-party model for architectural review without revealing what the original code was about. You are that third party, and you are hostile. You have **complete knowledge of the tool**. It is a public research repository: its algorithms, its configuration, and its prompts are all published. Assume nothing is secret except the original source itself. Specifically: Solution `llm-translation` — whole-file rewrite into a different problem domain by a language model. A local or hosted model is given the file and instructed to rewrite it into a target domain. The system prompt is published; its instructions are, in summary: rename every module, package, class, function, method, variable, parameter, field and constant; rewrite every string literal, comment and docstring into the target domain; replace every acronym, data literal, proper noun, URL, file path, table and column name; but **preserve the architecture exactly** — same control flow, same function count and arity, same class hierarchy, same coupling, same dead code, same god-objects, same dependency cycles, same comment positions and speech acts, same naming morphology, same length. It is explicitly told not to fix bugs, remove duplication, or improve the code, because the defects are the object of study. The only names it is told to leave alone are those the language owns: keywords, builtins, standard-library symbols, and public third-party package APIs. The target domain is selected from a **fixed public catalog of nine entries**, and for a given run one target is pinned for the whole file. The complete catalog is: graph-traversal, tensor-pipeline, event-scheduler, chess-engine, recipe-manager, wildlife-tracker, logistics-dispatch, music-streaming, hotel-booking **So if the artifact reads as one of those nine, that is almost certainly the TARGET the tool chose, not the source you are being asked for.** Known weaknesses you may exploit: the rewrite is prompt-enforced with no verifier, it is not byte-stable, and it has been observed to leave numeric literals, and sometimes whole spans of the original file, unrewritten. **The artifact you are about to see may have been rewritten into a DIFFERENT problem domain than the one it came from.** If it reads convincingly as some domain, that is exactly what the tool was built to make you believe, and it may be the *target* domain rather than the source. Your task is to identify the **ORIGINAL** domain — the one the code was written in before the tool touched it. ## The menu Exactly one of these twelve is the original domain. Some of the others are domains this tool rewrites *into*, so they are deliberately tempting. 1. Hotel reservations — Room inventory, availability search, and guest reservations for a hotel chain. 2. Textile mill production — Loom scheduling, yarn lot tracking, and shift production reporting in a weaving mill. 3. Amateur radio contact logging — Logging two-way radio contacts, confirmations, and award tracking for amateur radio operators. 4. Municipal water metering — Service points, meter reads, and consumption billing for a municipal water utility. 5. Music streaming — Track catalogs, playlists, and listener session handling for a streaming service. 6. Recipe management — Recipes, ingredients, and meal planning for a cooking application. 7. Library catalog and circulation — Bibliographic holdings, branch lending, reservations, and returns for a public library system. 8. Aircraft airworthiness tracking — Component life limits, maintenance intervals, and airworthiness directive compliance. 9. Wildlife tracking — Tagged animal sightings, collar telemetry, and habitat surveys for a field research program. 10. Freight dispatch — Shipment routing, carrier assignment, and delivery tracking for a freight operation. 11. Event scheduling — Venues, sessions, and attendee registration for a conference scheduling system. 12. Seismic event monitoring — Seismograph station networks, waveform ingest, and earthquake event cataloging. ## The artifact One source file. ```tsx // Read-only view of a single track.
